def: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. Osmosis is a special case of diffusion where only water molecules move through a semi-permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential.
points: Diffusion needs no membrane and no energy; it continues till concentration becomes equal everywhere.
Osmosis occurs only across a semi-permeable membrane, which allows water but not solute to pass.
Water moves from a dilute (high water potential) solution to a concentrated (low water potential) solution.
Endosmosis: water enters a cell placed in a hypotonic solution, cell swells.
Exosmosis: water leaves a cell placed in a hypertonic solution, cell shrinks.
In an isotonic solution there is no net movement of water, cell size stays the same.
Osmosis is important for water absorption by roots and turgidity of cells.
formula: Water potential, Psi(w) = Psi(s) + Psi(p) (solute potential + pressure potential)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Hypotonic solution"] --> B["Water moves in"]
  B --> C["Cell swells - Endosmosis"]
  D["Hypertonic solution"] --> E["Water moves out"]
  E --> F["Cell shrinks - Exosmosis"]

example: A raisin kept in plain water swells up because water enters it by endosmosis, since the raisin's cell contents are hypertonic to the surrounding water.
tip: Clearly distinguish diffusion from osmosis in a two-point table and mention the semi-permeable membrane condition for full marks.

def: Water potential (Psi(w)) is the free energy of water per unit volume, which determines the direction of water movement; it is the sum of solute potential and pressure potential.
points: Solute potential (Psi(s)) is always negative; it decreases as solute concentration increases.
Pressure potential (Psi(p)) is usually positive; it is the turgor pressure developed inside the cell wall.
Formula: Psi(w) = Psi(s) + Psi(p).
Pure water has water potential equal to zero (taken as reference).
Water always moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.
At full turgidity, Psi(p) equals the magnitude of Psi(s), so Psi(w) becomes zero and water movement stops.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Solute potential - negative"] --> C["Water potential"]
  B["Pressure potential - positive"] --> C
  C --> D["Water moves to lower water potential"]

example: If Psi(s) = -8 bar and Psi(p) = +5 bar, then Psi(w) = -8 + 5 = -3 bar.
tip: Always write the formula first and state sign conventions (Psi(s) negative, Psi(p) positive) — examiners check this specifically.

def: Plasmolysis is the shrinking of the protoplasm away from the cell wall when a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution and loses water by exosmosis.
points: Occurs when a living plant cell is kept in a strongly hypertonic (concentrated) solution.
Water moves out of the cell by exosmosis, following the water potential gradient.
The protoplast shrinks and separates from the rigid cell wall, which does not shrink.
This stage is called plasmolysis; the cell appears flaccid.
If the cell is then placed in water, water re-enters and the protoplast expands again — this is called deplasmolysis.
Plasmolysis proves that the cell membrane is living and semi-permeable.
formula: Exosmosis occurs when cell's Psi(w) is higher than outside solution's Psi(w)

diagram.draw: Draw a plant cell with a thick rectangular cell wall. Inside, draw the protoplast (cytoplasm with nucleus) shrunk away from the wall, leaving a gap. Label 'Cell wall', 'Shrunken protoplast', and 'Gap filled with external solution'.

example: An onion peel kept in 10% salt solution shows plasmolysed cells under a microscope within a few minutes.
tip: Mention that plasmolysis is reversible (deplasmolysis) — this extra point often fetches a bonus mark.

def: Absorption of water by roots is the process by which root hairs take up soil water and pass it inward to the xylem, mainly through osmosis and the apoplast/symplast pathways.
points: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorption and are in close contact with soil water.
Water enters root hair cells by osmosis because cell sap has lower (more negative) water potential than soil water.
Apoplast pathway: water moves through cell walls and intercellular spaces without crossing membranes.
Symplast pathway: water moves from cell to cell through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata.
At the endodermis, the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast path, forcing water through the symplast (membrane).
Water finally reaches the xylem vessels and moves upward.
formula: Water moves from higher Psi(w) in soil to lower Psi(w) in root cells

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Soil water"] --> B["Root hair"]
  B --> C["Cortex - apoplast and symplast"]
  C --> D["Endodermis - Casparian strip"]
  D --> E["Xylem vessel"]

example: Root hairs of a wheat seedling absorb soil water which travels through cortex cells and endodermis to reach the central xylem within minutes of watering.
tip: Draw the apoplast vs symplast pathway diagram and label the Casparian strip clearly — this is a favourite diagram question.

def: Ascent of sap is the upward movement of water and minerals from roots to leaves through the xylem, best explained by the cohesion-tension theory.
points: Transpiration from leaf surfaces creates a pull (tension) that is transmitted down the water column in the xylem.
Water molecules are held together by cohesion (hydrogen bonding), forming a continuous unbroken water column.
Water molecules also adhere to the walls of the narrow xylem vessels (adhesion), helping maintain the column.
Because of cohesion and adhesion, the tension created at the top pulls water all the way up from the roots.
This theory explains how water rises even in very tall trees without using metabolic energy.
Root pressure assists only in short plants and mainly at night when transpiration is low.
formula: Transpiration pull = Cohesion + Adhesion + Tension in the continuous water column

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Transpiration from leaf"] --> B["Creates tension/pull"]
  B --> C["Pull transmitted down xylem"]
  C --> D["Cohesion keeps water column unbroken"]
  D --> E["Water rises from root to leaf"]

example: In a tall tree 30 m high, the cohesion-tension mechanism alone can pull water upward without the plant spending ATP, powered purely by transpiration.
tip: Name the three components — cohesion, adhesion, tension — explicitly; examiners award separate marks for each term.

def: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from aerial plant parts, mostly through stomata, and is regulated by the opening and closing of guard cells.
points: Stomata are small pores on the leaf surface surrounded by two guard cells.
According to the K+ ion theory, guard cells actively accumulate potassium ions in daylight.
This lowers the water potential of guard cells, so water enters them by osmosis.
Guard cells become turgid; their thicker inner wall bows outward, opening the stomatal pore.
At night or under water stress, K+ ions move out, guard cells lose turgor, and the pore closes.
Transpiration helps in water movement, cooling the leaf, and mineral transport, but also causes water loss.
formula: High K+ in guard cells -> low Psi(w) -> water enters -> turgid guard cells -> stomata open

diagram.draw: Draw two bean-shaped guard cells facing each other with a stomatal pore between them. Show the inner wall (facing the pore) thicker than the outer wall. Label 'Guard cell', 'Stomatal pore', 'Thick inner wall', 'Thin outer wall', and 'K+ ions'.

example: On a sunny day, stomata of a potted plant stay open for photosynthesis, but the plant also loses a measurable amount of water as transpiration, visible as fogging under a bell jar experiment.
tip: Use the K+ ion theory, not the old starch-sugar theory, as the accepted mechanism — HSC answer keys expect this.
